accuracy.evidence: Checked against the dual coding research: Paivio's theory of separate verbal and imagery codes, Mayer's multimedia principle (words with relevant pictures beat words alone) and coherence principle (extra decoration can hurt learning), and Wammes, Meade and Fernandes 2016 on drawing improving recall. The plant parts and the seed, roots, shoot, flower order match Year 1 science, and the adult notes separate dual coding from the learning styles myth.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs that a thinking picture must be neat and coloured in (sketch prediction, How long should a sketch take question), that decoration makes a picture better (sparkle prediction, glitter stamp, decorated panels), that pictures are only for fun, and that a picture can replace the words. Each one has its own wrong option and reply.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagsketch lab is about pictures as thinking tools: stamping a two-item sketch on a page with glitter and rainbow stamps as distractors, labelling a drawn plant, adding pictures to word cards that draw a second path into a brain icon, a picture-card timeline drawn from seed to flower, and choosing between explain, decoration and off-topic panels. Highest shingle overlap with any other flag lab is 8.6 percent.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step shows one form of dual coding in action: the sketch step rewards the two shapes that show the idea and says the sparkles were not needed, labels join each word to a part, the cards step turns the cards over and makes the child use a picture clue to recall a word, and the timeline step makes order visible before the final pick-the-helpful-picture step.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before acting: whether a thinking picture must be neat and coloured in or quick and simple, whether a word on its own or a word with a picture is easier to remember, and whether lots of sparkle makes a picture more helpful. The done message after each task restates the locked guess and confirms or corrects it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions rotate their option order, and each wrong choice gets a specific reply, for example Neat colouring takes time but does not explain more, quick shapes and labels are enough, and Keep the words too, words and picture together work best. A streak counter and an Another button let a child keep practising.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences (Add labels. A label is a word that names a part.) within the family reading limit, and lab prompts are short commands a six year old can follow. The adult notes name the research in plain words and use the curriculum terms labelled diagram, timeline and parts of flowering plants.

no_filler.evidence: Every adult paragraph carries content: the research basis with named authors and year, where the three forms appear in the Year 1 to 4 curriculum, three named mistakes plus the learning styles caution, and a step-by-step description of the lab. The family tip gives a concrete three-box story drawing and a one-minute labelled sketch routine.

mobile.evidence: The lab uses the young layout with 56 pixel buttons, every canvas tap target also has a button in the control row, and the sketch stamps can be tapped to drop into place instead of dragged. Screens on iPhone 13 and Android in light and dark themes keep the cards, plant labels, timeline and three panels inside the canvas without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas aria-label follows each spoken instruction, every control has a descriptive label such as Label the roots or Choose picture B, the Challenge answers sit in a labelled group with a polite live status, and the browser gate ran axe in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations.
